lead: A wide adder is slow because the carry must reach the last bit. Three architectures attack that chain without changing the final arithmetic. Carry select computes each block twice, with carry in 0 and 1, then selects. Carry skip passes the carry over a block whose bits all propagate. Carry save never propagates the carry inside a row: it keeps a sum vector and a carry vector for a later adder. The names CSL, CSK and CSA appear in datapath and multiplier design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the full adder and for generate g and propagate p.

blocks.text: Carry select splits an n-bit adder into blocks of k bits. Each block contains two ripple adders. One assumes its carry in is 0. The other assumes 1. Both run at the same time.

For each sum bit in the block, a multiplexer picks the output of the correct adder. The select signal is the real carry coming from the lower block. The carry out of the block is also selected. No sum bit waits for the lower block; only the final selection waits.

For a = 1011 and b = 0110 in two-bit blocks, the low block gives sum 01 with carry 1. The high block (10 + 01) gives sum 11, carry 0 for carry-in 0 and sum 00, carry 1 for carry-in 1. The real carry 1 selects the second: 1 00 01 = 10001 = 17 (Figure 4.2.1).

Area is the cost. A carry-select block needs four full adders plus three 2:1 multiplexers: two for the sum bits and one for the carry out. The first block has no choice to make, so it is a single ripple adder. With equal blocks of k bits, every block ripples at the same time (k carry delays), then the real carry steps through one multiplexer per block, n/k − 1 of them. The square-root carry-select adder makes each block one bit longer than the block below it (2, 3, 4, 5 …), so a block's two answers are ready just as the selected carry reaches it. Its delay then grows roughly as √(2n) multiplexer delays, while the area stays proportional to n, close to double a plain ripple adder. The carry skip adder below is also called a square-root adder; the two are different architectures.

sections.h3: Carry skip: bypass a propagating block

blocks.text: Carry skip, also called carry bypass, uses the propagate signal p<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub> XOR b<sub>i</sub> from Chapter 4.1. A bit propagates a carry when p<sub>i</sub> = 1: a carry in produces a carry out. For a block from bit m to bit n, define block propagate P = p<sub>m</sub> · p<sub>m+1</sub> · ... · p<sub>n</sub>. The dot means AND.

If P = 1, every bit in the block propagates. Any carry entering the block will leave it unchanged. A multiplexer then sends the incoming carry straight to the next block, bypassing the ripple chain. If P = 0, at least one bit stops or generates a carry, so the block uses its normal ripple carry out.

The block size k sets the delay. In the worst case a carry is generated at the bottom of the lowest block and ripples through its k bits, then jumps over the middle blocks through one bypass multiplexer each, and finally ripples through the k bits of the top block. With t<sub>c</sub> the carry delay of one bit and t<sub>mux</sub> the delay of one bypass multiplexer:

Here n is the adder width in bits; k is the block width in bits; 2k·t<sub>c</sub> is the ripple in the first and last blocks; n/k − 1 is the number of bypass multiplexers on the path; k<sub>opt</sub> is where the two terms balance (set dT/dk = 0).

Small blocks skip often but put many multiplexers in the path; large blocks ripple too far. With t<sub>c</sub> = t<sub>mux</sub>, a 32-bit adder has k<sub>opt</sub> = √16 = 4 and about 15 delays, against 32 for plain ripple (worked example 2). The skip logic is cheap: one AND of the block's p bits and one 2:1 multiplexer per block.

sections.h3: Carry save: keep the carry for later

blocks.text: A carry save adder does not try to finish the sum. It takes three numbers and reduces them to two. Each column uses one full adder as a 3:2 compressor. The full adder adds three input bits at the same position and produces a sum bit s<sub>i</sub> and a carry bit c<sub>i</sub>. The carry bit belongs one place to the left.

For inputs a, b and d, the row produces S = s<sub>n-1</sub>...s<sub>0</sub> and raw carry bits c<sub>n-1</sub>...c<sub>0</sub>. The arithmetic identity is a + b + d = S + 2C, where C is the raw carry word c<sub>n-1</sub>...c<sub>0</sub>. In hardware the shifted carry vector is C' = 2C, so a + b + d = S + C'. A final carry propagate adder, such as the ripple or look-ahead adder of Chapter 4.1, adds S and C'. That final adder is the only place where a carry ripples.

The delay of the compressor row is one full adder delay. There is no carry chain across columns. The price is the final adder. In a multiplier, many partial-product rows are reduced by a tree of these 3:2 compressors. Wallace tree multipliers, often fed by Booth-recoded partial products, are built from exactly this block; see Chapter 4.4.

spec.aria: Two ripple adders for the high block with carry in 0 and 1, a low-block adder whose carry selects the multiplexers, and the result 10001.

examples.question: Use one row of carry save adders to add a = 1011 (11), b = 0110 (6) and d = 0101 (5). Give the sum vector S, the shifted carry vector C, and the final sum after the carry propagate adder.
steps: Column 0: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, so s0 = 0 and raw carry c0 = 1.
Column 1: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so s1 = 0 and raw carry c1 = 1.
Column 2: 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, so s2 = 0 and raw carry c2 = 1.
Column 3: 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, so s3 = 1 and raw carry c3 = 0.
Sum vector S = s3 s2 s1 s0 = 1000 binary = 8.
Raw carry word = c3 c2 c1 c0 = 0111 binary = 7.
Shift the carry word left by one bit: C = 1110 binary = 14.
Final carry propagate add: S + C = 8 + 14 = 22. Check: 11 + 6 + 5 = 22.
examples.answer: S = 1000 (8), shifted carry C = 1110 (14), and the final sum is 10110 binary (22), which equals 11 + 6 + 5.
examples.check:
a = 0b1011
b = 0b0110
d = 0b0101
S = 0
C = 0
for i in range(4):
    total = ((a >> i) & 1) + ((b >> i) & 1) + ((d >> i) & 1)
    s = total & 1
    carry = total >> 1
    S |= s << i
    C |= carry << i
print(S)
print(C << 1)
print(S + (C << 1))

examples.question: A 32-bit carry skip adder is built from equal blocks. One bit's carry delay is t<sub>c</sub> = 1 unit and one bypass multiplexer is t<sub>mux</sub> = 1 unit. Find the worst-case delay for k = 2, 4 and 8, pick the best block size, and compare with a plain 32-bit ripple adder.
steps: k = 2: 16 blocks, T = 4 + 15 = 19 units. k = 4: 8 blocks, T = 8 + 7 = 15 units. k = 8: 4 blocks, T = 16 + 3 = 19 units.
Optimum: k<sub>opt</sub> = √(n·t<sub>mux</sub> ÷ 2t<sub>c</sub>) = √(32 ÷ 2) = 4, which matches the table.
Plain ripple: 32 stages × 1 unit = 32 units. Speed-up = 32 ÷ 15 ≈ 2.1.
examples.answer: k = 4 is best at about 15 units, against 19 units for k = 2 or k = 8 and 32 units for plain ripple; the bypass logic costs only eight AND gates and eight multiplexers.

traps: Forgetting to shift the carry vector left by one bit before the final add. The raw carry word 0111 is 7, but the shifted vector 1110 is 14.
Expecting a carry save adder to produce a finished sum on its own. It only reduces three inputs to two vectors; a final carry propagate adder is still needed.
Using OR instead of AND for block propagate P in a carry skip adder. A carry crosses the whole block only when every p<sub>i</sub> is 1.
In carry select, the multiplexer select is the real carry from the lower block, not the block's own carry out. Both candidate carries are already computed.

quiz.a: CSL is carry select, CSK is carry skip (carry bypass), and CSA is carry save adder.

quiz.q: Why does a carry save adder not give a finished sum?
quiz.a: It produces a sum vector S and a carry vector C without propagating carries across columns. The final value is S + 2C, so a carry propagate adder must add S and the shifted carry vector.

quiz.q: A carry save row gives S = 00101100 (44) and shifted carry C = 00011010 (26). What is the final sum?
For a 32-bit carry skip adder with t<sub>c</sub> = t<sub>mux</sub> = 1 delay unit, compare k = 4 and k = 8 using T ≈ 2k·t<sub>c</sub> + (32/k − 1)·t<sub>mux</sub>. Which block size is faster?
quiz.a: k = 4: 2·4 + (8 − 1) = 8 + 7 = 15 units. k = 8: 2·8 + (4 − 1) = 16 + 3 = 19 units. k = 4 is faster by 4 units, as k<sub>opt</sub> = √(32 ÷ 2) = 4 predicts.

quiz.q: Carry select uses two ripple adders per block, yet it is faster. Explain why.
quiz.a: Both adders compute in parallel before the lower-block carry is ready. When the real carry arrives, a multiplexer selects one of two ready results. The delay becomes one block ripple plus multiplexer delay, not a carry chain through all n bits. The cost is extra area.

beyond: Not for the exam. Carry-save rows sit inside every multiplier tree and dot-product unit, and synthesis tools pick among adder structures automatically for each timing target. Search for "prefix adder" and "redundant number system".
